title: "Rasters on S3"
---

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
```

Satellite archives live in object storage, and the pipelines that consume them increasingly
write their outputs back there too. `freezecore.raster` exists so that reading and writing
those rasters looks the same whether the file is on local disk or in a bucket.

## The problem it solves

`rasterio` can already open an `s3://` URI — GDAL's `/vsis3/` driver handles it. What it
cannot do is work out *which* credentials to use. That is configured through GDAL
environment variables (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_S3_ENDPOINT`, `AWS_NO_SIGN_REQUEST`, and
a dozen more), set globally, at a different layer from the path you are opening.

The result is code that carries credentials in one place and paths in another, and breaks
in confusing ways when a pipeline touches two different object stores in one process.

`freezecore` attaches the credentials to the path itself. `make_s3_upath()` builds a
`UPath` that carries its storage options, and `rasterio_open()` reads those options back
out and installs them into a GDAL environment for exactly the duration of the `with`
block:

```python
from freezecore.raster import rasterio_open
from freezecore.s3 import make_s3_upath

path = make_s3_upath("s3://my-bucket/scene.tif", key=..., secret=...)
with rasterio_open(path) as src:
    data = src.read(1)
```

Because the configuration travels with the path, two stores in the same process do not
interfere, and `rasterio_open()` is otherwise a drop-in replacement for `rasterio.open()`
— a plain `Path` or `str` opens a local file with no S3 machinery involved.

::: {.callout-note}
## Requires the `s3` extra

`freezecore.s3` needs `s3fs`, `fsspec`, and `boto3`. Install with
`pip install "freezecore[s3] @ git+https://github.com/lqgentner/freezecore.git"`. The
import is lazy, so `freezecore.raster` works for local files without the extra.
:::

## A real, public example

The [Copernicus DEM GLO-30](https://registry.opendata.aws/copernicus-dem/) is a global
30 m elevation model published on the AWS Open Data registry. The bucket is public, so
omitting `key` and `secret` sends unsigned requests and no account is needed:

```{python}
from freezecore.raster import rasterio_open
from freezecore.s3 import make_s3_upath

# GLO-30 is tiled into 1° x 1° COGs named by their south-west corner.
tile = "Copernicus_DSM_COG_10_N46_00_E008_00_DEM"
dem_path = make_s3_upath(
    f"s3://copernicus-dem-30m/{tile}/{tile}.tif",
    region="eu-central-1",
)

with rasterio_open(dem_path) as src:
    print(f"driver:     {src.driver}")
    print(f"crs:        {src.crs}")
    print(f"shape:      {src.shape}")
    print(f"dtype:      {src.dtypes[0]}")
    print(f"bounds:     {tuple(round(v) for v in src.bounds)}")
    print(f"overviews:  {src.overviews(1)}")
```

Note what the source looks like: geographic coordinates (EPSG:4326), 3600 × 3600 pixels
spanning a whole degree, with a pixel size in fractions of a degree rather than metres.
It is a perfectly good DEM and completely unusable as a stacking target.

## Resampling onto a grid square

This is where the [MGRS grid](01-mgrs-grid.qmd) pays off. An `MGRSGeoBox` carries the
three things `rasterio.warp.reproject` needs for its destination — `crs`, `transform`,
and `shape` — so the resampling call needs no other geospatial arguments:

```{python}
import numpy as np
from rasterio.warp import Resampling, reproject

from freezecore.mgrs import MGRSGeoBox

square = MGRSGeoBox.from_mgrs("32TMS35", resolution=10.0)

dem = np.full(square.shape.yx, np.nan, dtype="float32")
with rasterio_open(dem_path) as src:
    reproject(
        source=src.read(1),
        destination=dem,
        src_transform=src.transform,
        src_crs=src.crs,
        dst_transform=square.transform,
        dst_crs=square.crs,
        dst_nodata=np.nan,
        resampling=Resampling.bilinear,
    )

print(f"{square.mgrs_code}: {dem.shape} px @ {square.resolution.x} m in {square.crs}")
print(f"elevation: {np.nanmin(dem):.0f} m - {np.nanmax(dem):.0f} m")
```

The DEM is now a 1000 × 1000 array in EPSG:32632 at exactly 10 m — the same array shape,
CRS, and transform that every other source resampled onto `32TMS35` will have. That is the
entire point of fixing the grid first.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Copernicus DEM GLO-30 resampled onto MGRS grid square 32TMS35 (Fiescher/Aletsch area, Bernese Alps) at 10 m."
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

left, bottom, right, top = square.boundingbox
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 5.5))
im = ax.imshow(dem, cmap="terrain", extent=(left, right, bottom, top))
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="elevation (m)", shrink=0.85)
ax.set_title(f"MGRS {square.mgrs_code}")
ax.set_xlabel("easting (m)")
ax.set_ylabel("northing (m)")
ax.ticklabel_format(style="plain")
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Pick squares that fit their source tile

GLO-30 tiles are 1° × 1°, and MGRS squares do not respect degree boundaries. `32TMS35`
happens to sit entirely inside the `N46/E008` tile; a square straddling 8° E would need
both neighbouring tiles, leaving a nodata stripe if only one is read. `merge_tiffs()`
handles that case, or read the sources through a `rasterio.vrt.WarpedVRT` mosaic.
:::

## Writing the result back

`write_cog()` takes the array straight to a Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF, staging through an
in-memory file and applying `COG_PROFILE`'s compression and overview settings. Again the
`GeoBox` supplies the georeferencing:

```{python}
#| eval: false
from freezecore.raster import write_cog

profile = {
    "dtype": "float32",
    "count": 1,
    "width": square.shape.x,
    "height": square.shape.y,
    "crs": square.crs,
    "transform": square.transform,
    "nodata": np.nan,
}

write_cog(dem, f"dem_{square.mgrs_code}.tif", profile, band_names=["elevation"])
```

The destination may equally be an S3 `UPath`, in which case the object is written with a
single atomic `PutObject`:

```python
dst = make_s3_upath(f"s3://my-bucket/dem/{square.mgrs_code}.tif", key=..., secret=...)
write_cog(dem, dst, profile, band_names=["elevation"])
```

For files that already exist, `rewrite_tiff()` does the same job without loading the array
yourself — recompressing, retiling, renaming bands, or moving between backends. Source and
destination credentials are resolved independently, so S3-to-S3 copies across two
different stores work:

```python
from freezecore.raster import COG_PROFILE, rewrite_tiff

rewrite_tiff("scene.tif", dst, profile=COG_PROFILE)             # local -> S3, as COG
rewrite_tiff(src_on_store_a, dst_on_store_b, move=True)         # S3 -> S3, then delete
```

## Listing objects

One gap worth knowing about. `make_s3_upath()` configures anonymous access for *GDAL*, via
`rasterio_open()`, but it has no `anon` passthrough to `s3fs`. Filesystem-level operations
on the returned path — `.exists()`, `.iterdir()`, `.glob()` — therefore still try to sign
their requests and fail on a public bucket with `NoCredentialsError`.

Until that is exposed, use a plain `UPath` with `anon=True` for listing:

```{python}
from upath import UPath

bucket = UPath("s3://copernicus-dem-30m/", anon=True)
[p.name for p in list(bucket.iterdir())[:3]]
```

Reading is unaffected — `rasterio_open()` on a `make_s3_upath()` path works anonymously,
as everything above this section demonstrates.

## Related helpers

`freezecore.raster` carries a few more utilities that come up in the same pipelines:

| Function | Use |
|---|---|
| `merge_tiffs()` | Mosaic several GeoTIFFs, grouping by CRS |
| `group_tiffs_by_crs()` | Partition a file list by CRS before merging |
| `build_rasterio_profile()` | Merge profile dicts onto sensible defaults |
| `get_utm_zone_string()` / `utm_zone_to_crs()` | Convert between UTM zone strings and CRS |

See the [API reference](../reference/index.qmd) for full signatures.
